title: The Dream of Print
thesis: The dream of multiplying the written word, read as a fork from one root. From East Asian woodblock the craft branches: West, it turns to metal — movable type and the copperplate meeting in Gutenberg's press, through publishing and the steam press to offset, and text becomes everyone's; East, the block stays a block, crosses to Japan as the people's ukiyo-e, and through Japonisme reshapes Art Nouveau — the birth of commercial design. Two dreams of the multiplied image, from one carved page.

scenes.description: Woodblock printing (China, Tang dynasty) — whole pages carved into wood and inked; the Diamond Sutra of 868 is the earliest dated printed book. The common root: from here the craft forks — West toward metal and the press, East staying with the block.

scenes.description: Johannes Gutenberg (Mainz, c.1440) — a press with cast metal type, oil-based ink and the screw press; the 42-line Bible (c.1455). Movable type and metal-plate craft converge; mechanised printing ignites Europe's knowledge revolution.

scenes.description: Aldus Manutius (Venice, c.1500) — italic type and the portable octavo book; the printer as publisher. The dream turns from making pages to making readers — the birth of modern publishing.

scenes.description: Ira Rubel's offset lithography (1904) — the image is offset from plate to rubber blanket to paper; fast, cheap, universal. The Western branch's modern end: the world printed at scale.

scenes.description: Ukiyo-e (Japan, Edo through 幕末) — woodblock carried east and kept, flowering into a secular, commercial print culture: colour prints of actors, courtesans, and landscapes sold cheaply to the townspeople. The block becomes a people's mass medium.

scenes.description: Art Nouveau (Europe, c.1890–1910) — through Japonisme, ukiyo-e's flat colour, bold outline and asymmetry remake Western design (Mucha's posters, Toulouse-Lautrec). The East branch's fruit: the birth of modern commercial and graphic design.
